title: Savings sprint: batching & KV cost walkthrough - Venari Labs
summary: Redwood AE + SE ran an Optimize console walkthrough focused on batching and prefix/KV cache recommendations tied to a customized cost model. Venari shared their latency SLOs (p95 < 200ms), session patterns (sporadic bursts with long conversations), and on-prem constraints. The call covered prefetch heuristics, TTL sizing, concurrency effects on batching, fallback routing, and an initial savings simulation. Agreed next steps: Redwood to send tailored cost spreadsheet, set up a 2-week pilot sandbox, and run a small benchmark with Venari sample traffic.
next_steps: Redwood: share cost-model spreadsheet and playbook links (due 2026-08-03)
Venari: provide 24h sample of production traces & typical prompt/token distributions (due 2026-08-05)
Schedule pilot kickoff (2-week sandbox) - action: Maya to propose times

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-31
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE); Jon Patel (Redwood SE); Aisha Rahman (Venari, Head of ML); Tom Rivera (Venari, SRE); Priya Nair (Venari, Product)

Auto-summary: walkthrough of Optimize console recommendations for batching and prefix/K-V cache (note: transcript auto-captions sometimes show 'K-V cash' or 'Redwood Optimizer').

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account, joining with Jon our SE. How are you all?
[00:08] Aisha: Doing well, thanks. Busy week but excited to dig in, we want to understand concrete econ saves for our anomaly detection product.
[00:14] Jon: Great. Quick agenda — we’ll run through your current patterns, demo the Optimize console savings sim, then walk through batching + prefix/KV prefetch heuristics and recommended TTLs. We'll finish with next steps. Sound good?
[00:27] Tom: Yep, that works. Our main constraints: p95 latency under 200ms for interactive sessions, we have a mix of long sessions and quick lookups, and we run a hybrid: some on-prem GPUs, some hosted.
[00:40] Priya: Also want to keep data residency for EU users — so we might need VPC/private placement for certain routes.

[02:05] Jon: Cool. Can you give a quick picture of traffic patterns — bursts vs steady state, average tokens per session?
[02:13] Aisha: Sure. Roughly 60% of traffic is short queries (10-30 tokens) for routing/metadata, 40% are longer sessions — avg 800 tokens per session, but we have spikes during nightly analysis where batch requests come in.
[02:28] Maya: Thanks. That mix is actually one of the cases where prefix/KV prefetch helps — for long sessions the KV cache reduces repeated forward work, and for short queries batching can help at scale.

[04:00] Jon: Opening the Optimize console — note the 'savings simulator' panel on the right. We loaded a mock of Venari's distribution and configured three levers: batch size target, prefetch ratio, and TTL. I'll toggle prefetch from off to conservative to aggressive.
[04:24] Jon: With prefetch off, baseline token cost per 1k requests is X — we see small batching wins but no reuse. Turn conservative prefetch (prefix length 128, prefetch probability 0.3) — CPU/GPU load increases a bit but per-token cost drops ~18% in the sim. Aggressive (prefetch 0.8, lookahead 512) pushes reuse further but you pay for extra generator tokens and slightly higher latency in tail cases.
[05:10] Aisha: Is that the lookahead reading the next 512 tokens? I guess that might be heavy for us on on-prem nodes.
[05:17] Jon: Right, lookahead is speculative generation to populate KV cache; it's optional and we show latency impact. On dedicated GPUs you can usually push more aggressive lookahead. For on-prem we recommend conservative lookahead and stronger TTL logic.

[07:05] Priya: Can you clarify TTL sizing? What's the tradeoff between a long TTL and eviction pressure?
[07:15] Jon: TTL controls how long a cached KV is kept. Longer TTL increases cache hit rate (and thus saves compute) but can increase memory usage on the inference nodes and also risk serving stale context if your prefix semantics change. We usually set TTL to session duration percentiles — e.g., if 95% of sessions are under 30 minutes, TTL 30m is a good start.
[07:40] Tom: We have strict memory budgets per node — what about evict-on-memory-pressure strategies?
[07:48] Jon: We support LRU and weighted-LRU where longer sequences are evicted first, plus a soft TTL that expires entries unless recently used. In the console we demo the hit-rate curve with your dataset to pick a TTL that stays within memory budget.

[10:02] Maya: Let's run a quick sensitivity sim — Jon, can you toggle concurrency up to 8 and reduce batch target to 16?
[10:08] Jon: Doing that now — as concurrency increases, batching windows tighten because of interleaving, so effective batch size drops if requests are bursty. But with session affinity and sticky routing we can keep batch efficiency high for multiplayer sessions. See the sim: with concurrency 8 and session affinity on, cost per token drops ~12% versus affinity off.
[11:00] Aisha: Session affinity — that means we route the same session to the same instance so the KV lives local?
[11:07] Jon: Exactly. It's a tradeoff: affinity improves cache hit rates and batching locality but reduces global load balancing flexibility. For Venari's long conversational sessions it's often worthwhile.

[13:45] Priya: We're also worried about privacy/compliance for EU customers. If we route to regional nodes are you able to enforce KMS per-region?
[13:52] Maya: Yes, Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and regional control planes. We can map routes by geo and enforce encryption keys per region — we'll attach SOC2/ISO docs after the call.
[14:05] Tom: Great, please add that to the security packet.

[16:20] Jon: Back to caching heuristics — two quick approaches we recommend: 1) prefix-based prefetch with conservative lookahead for long sessions, 2) short-query batching with stateless micro-batching and aggressive batch sizes for metadata lookup paths. The console can apply both rules to routes.
[16:40] Aisha: For the prefix prefetch, do you precompute on write or on first read? We're worried about unnecessary generator runs.
[16:49] Jon: It's read-time prefetching by default — it only generates additional tokens when a matching prefix is seen. You can also schedule background prefetch for sessions predicted to continue (we call that predictive prefetch). Predictive prefetch trades generator compute for improved next-step latency.

[19:10] Maya: Let's show the cost breakdown chart — tokens, GPU-time, idle overhead, and the amortized KV hit savings.
[19:20] Jon: Here. For your sample distribution, prefetch conservative reduces GPU time by 21% but increases total tokens due to lookahead by ~6%. Net unit cost down ~15%. If you enable session affinity and increase batch target from 16 to 32 during off-peak you can push savings to ~22%.
[19:55] Priya: Off-peak batching — we have nightly bulk analysis windows. Can the runtime auto-switch policies?
[20:03] Jon: Yes — routing policies support schedule-based and load-based switching, e.g., auto-increase batching during low-latency sensitivity windows. We have a demo in the console for policy rules.

[22:40] Tom: Any reliability concerns — e.g., cache corruption or cold-start anomalies?
[22:48] Jon: We keep KV cache versioned per model version. If you roll models we'll warm the cache for pinned sessions and we offer automatic fallback to a cheaper model if a node fails. Cache integrity is logged and you can export audit traces. Some transcriber notes: sometimes log labels show 'KV cash' which is meaningless but ignore that.

[25:00] Aisha: Can we walk through an example with our tokens/sample?
[25:07] Jon: Sure, I uploaded a 24h sample you sent earlier — note the hit-rate curve on the left. For prefixes longer than 64 tokens our simulated hit rate is ~38% with TTL 30m, but for prefix 256 it's ~52%. That guides the lookahead decisions.
[26:00] Maya: Important callout — the console's simulator assumes typical KV-key cardinality; if you have lots of unique session prefixes (low reuse) then prefetch has less impact. What's your effective prefix cardinality?
[26:12] Aisha: We have medium cardinality — repeated users, but a lot of dynamic session metadata. We'll push a sanitized sample after the call.

[28:30] Jon: Discussing eviction policy — we recommend weighted-LRU with a TTL floor so very recent sessions are kept even if memory pressure occurs. That keeps high-value sessions available.
[29:10] Tom: About instrumentation — can we get token-level traces per-route?
[29:18] Maya: Yes, the Console gives token-level cost breakdown and you can export traces to your SIEM. We can also enable 30-day or 90-day retention for audit logs as an add-on.

[31:05] Priya: What about fallback routing to smaller models in case of capacity exhaustion? I want graceful degradation, not hard failures.
[31:13] Jon: Redwood supports fallback chains — you can define route A -> model X (primary) and fallback to model Y (cheaper) with a maximum latency budget. We also provide automatic circuit-breaker rules.

[33:40] Aisha: For the pilot, what's the minimal instrumentation you need to show value?
[33:47] Maya: Ideally a 24–72h sample plus a small sandbox traffic replay. We'll run the console sim, then a live micro-benchmark (1000 sessions) to measure real hit rates. Jon will stand up the sandbox config with the prefetch primitives.

[35:55] Jon: Quick note on batching windows — we support continuous batching where the runtime aggregates tokens across microseconds to maximize GPU utilization without adding large latency. If your p95 is tight, we reduce hold windows and lean on KV savings.
[36:20] Tom: So continuous batching won't break our 200ms p95?
[36:24] Jon: With the right parameters, no — the runtime keeps latency SLOs by adjusting batch thresholds and preferring local cache hits. The simulator includes a latency sensitivity toggle to preview tail spikes.

[38:50] Maya: Let's capture a short recap. Aisha — your success criteria again?
[38:56] Aisha: Reduce per-request cost by at least 15% while keeping p95 < 200ms and maintaining EU residency. Also want to avoid significant memory budget increases per node.
[39:07] Maya: Great. Agreed deliverables: cost-model spreadsheet from us, sandbox for a 2-week pilot, Venari sample traffic, and security docs.

[41:00] Priya: Any blockers on our side for pilot? We may need legal to sign the sandbox NDA.
[41:07] Maya: We can send a standard pilot agreement; legal review usually takes 3–5 business days.

[43:30] Tom: A couple of small questions — if we use predictive prefetch, can we throttle it on nodes that are memory constrained?
[43:38] Jon: Yes, predictive prefetch is tunable per-node and per-route. You can cap lookahead tokens and disable it in constrained clusters.
[44:05] Aisha: Ok that sounds workable.
[44:11] Maya: I'll send the spreadsheet and links. Jon will provision the sandbox and outline the on-call plan. We'll aim to reconvene after you ingest the sample — propose 2026-08-10 for pilot kickoff?
[44:28] Aisha: Works for us.
[44:30] Maya: Awesome, thanks everyone. End call.

Post-call notes: shared links promised: https://console.redwood.ai/optimize/savings-sim (demo view), security packet (SOC2/ISO) link placeholder, cost-model spreadsheet (to be shared). Some transcript noise: 'K-V cash' appears in automated captions in a few places, 'Redwood Optimiser' also appears.
